claims.text: Plastic deformation in quaternary equiatomic FCC alloys is primarily governed by dislocation glide at temperatures above 300 K.
At cryogenic temperatures, deformation twinning and FCC-to-HCP transformation become the dominant deformation mechanisms.
Cryogenic twinning and FCC-to-HCP transformation enhance both strength and ductility.
Yield strength becomes insensitive to strain rate above 800 K.
Above 800 K, dislocation climb and grain-boundary sliding dominate over athermal dislocation glide.
The initial material is a homogeneous, single-phase FCC quaternary equiatomic solid solution, exemplified by Co-Cr-Fe-Ni.
Uniaxial tension will be applied from 77 K to 1273 K at strain rates from 10^-4 to 10^2 s^-1 in vacuum or an inert atmosphere.
Dislocation cells, wavy or zigzag dislocations, deformation twins, and FCC-HCP interfaces evolve with temperature and strain.
Low-temperature TWIP and TRIP arise because chemical short-range order and lattice friction hinder dislocation motion.
Thermal activation of dislocation glide and twin-boundary mobility mediates the transition between low- and high-temperature mechanisms.
Yield strength increases as temperature decreases because TWIP and TRIP become more prominent.
Ductility peaks at cryogenic temperatures because deformation twinning delays necking.
At low temperatures and high strains, FCC-to-HCP transformation contributes to work hardening.
Conventional FCC pure metals and binary alloys deform primarily by dislocation glide across all temperatures and have minimal twinning or phase-transformation contributions.
The hypothesis applies to single-phase equiatomic FCC alloys with moderate to high stacking-fault energy.
The hypothesis may not apply to multiphase alloys, BCC alloys, or very-low-stacking-fault-energy alloys in which martensitic transformation dominates.
The transition temperature depends on alloy composition and stacking-fault energy.
Grain size and texture can influence high-temperature strain-rate insensitivity.
The appearance of HCP diffraction peaks or twin-related diffraction features during cryogenic tension would distinguish transformation or twinning from deformation solely by dislocation glide.
Constant yield strength across strain rates at 800 K would confirm diffusion-controlled deformation, whereas significant rate dependence would falsify the strain-rate-insensitivity hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis assigns dislocation glide as the primary mechanism throughout temperatures above 300 K, while the mechanism field assigns diffusion-controlled climb and grain-boundary sliding as dominant above 800 K; these temperature domains overlap.
Strain-rate insensitivity is predicted for temperatures above 800 K, but the proposed test is conducted at exactly 800 K, which lies outside the stated strict boundary.
